chief_complaint: unilateral calf pain, swelling, and warmth
hpi_details: A 38-year-old female presents to the clinic with unilateral calf pain, swelling, and warmth. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she pulled a calf muscle or tore a tendon while doing a workout class earlier this week.
concerns: She is worried that she will be unable to walk or travel for an important business conference next week.
expectations: She hopes to get an ultrasound or scan of her leg and leave with an elastic compression bandage and pain relievers.

investigation_events.title: Urgent lower-extremity compression ultrasound
investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent compression ultrasound result is now available.

results.value: Noncompressible thrombus extending from the popliteal vein into the distal femoral vein with absent color flow

clinical_knowledge.topic: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management for Deep Vein Thrombosis emphasizes anticoagulation (apixaban / warfarin) and compression ultrasound, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: unilateral calf pain, swelling, and warmth

Key HPI features: A 38-year-old female presents to the clinic with unilateral calf pain, swelling, and warmth. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Deep Vein Thrombosis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cellulitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Chest pain or shortness of breath — possible pulmonary embolism.
management_principles: Plan for Deep Vein Thrombosis: Anticoagulation (Apixaban / Warfarin), compression ultrasound
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of unilateral calf pain, swelling, and warmth. HPI: hypercoagulability, prolonged immobility.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Deep Vein Thrombosis.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Deep Vein Thrombosis.
reference_soap.plan: Assess pretest probability and obtain compression ultrasonography promptly. Start anticoagulation after confirmation, or before imaging only when clinical suspicion is high and imaging will be delayed with acceptable bleeding risk. Select the anticoagulant based on patient factors rather than routinely defaulting to warfarin.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Deep Vein Thrombosis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Deep Vein Thrombosis
Implement evidence-based management plan: Anticoagulation (Apixaban / Warfarin), compression ultrasound

teaching.one_liner: A clot forms in a deep leg vein, often from prolonged immobility, causing unilateral calf pain, swelling, and warmth.
red_flags: Chest pain or shortness of breath — possible pulmonary embolism

must_ask.say: Have you been immobile recently, or had surgery?
Is the swelling in just one leg?
When did the swelling and pain start?
Any chest pain or trouble breathing?
Have you ever had a blood clot before?

history.answer: My right calf has been swollen, warm, and painful for the last few days, and it feels like it's getting worse.
The swelling is just in my right calf and lower leg. My left leg, face, and belly look completely normal.
It started three days ago as a dull ache, and the swelling and tightness have been steadily increasing since then.
It is a constant throbbing ache that gets sharper when I stand up or walk. Resting with my leg up helps take some pressure off.
My right calf feels hot to the touch and looks somewhat red, but my left calf feels completely cool and normal.
It stays swollen all day and all night. It doesn't disappear when I wake up in the morning.
Yes, when I push on my right shin it leaves a small dent, and my sock leaves a tight dent in my skin that takes a long time to go away.
No, my weight has been completely steady at around sixty kilograms.
Four days ago, I returned from a fourteen-hour direct flight from Europe, and I slept in my seat almost the entire time without walking around.
No, I have not had any shortness of breath, chest tightness, or trouble catching my breath.
No chest pain, no palpitations, and no cough or coughing up blood.
No, I can lie completely flat without any breathing problems, and I haven't woken up gasping at night.
No, my urine looks normal pale yellow with no blood, foam, or decrease in amount.
No, my stomach has not grown larger, my eyes and skin are not yellow, and I haven't noticed easy bruising or bleeding gums.
No, I haven't had a sore throat, fever, or any cuts, scrapes, or bug bites on my leg.
No, I didn't twist my leg, slip, or do any strenuous exercise before this started.
I have felt generalized fatigue over the last few days, but I haven't had any cold sensitivity, dry skin, or constipation.
My appetite is good, and I haven't had any diarrhea, vomiting, or unintended weight loss.
I don't eat particularly salty foods, but at work I do sit at my computer desk for six to eight hours a day.
No, I have never had a blood clot, DVT, or vein issue before.
I don't have any chronic illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease, or kidney trouble.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medicines, over-the-counter pain relievers, or vitamins.
No, I do not have any known drug or food allergies.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used e-cigarettes.
I drink socially once or twice a month, usually a glass of beer or wine, and I don't have hepatitis.
I work as an office administrator and live in an apartment with my husband.
No one in my immediate family has a history of blood clots, pulmonary embolisms, heart attacks, or kidney failure.
My periods are regular every twenty-eight days, and my last period began two weeks ago. We use condoms and I am definitely not pregnant.
I thought I just pulled a muscle or tore something in my calf during my workout class a few days ago.

I have a major work conference next week where I have to be on my feet, and I'm worried I won't even be able to walk. I was hoping you could do an ultrasound to make sure nothing is torn and give me a compression wrap and some painkillers.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, pulse 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, body temperature 36.8°C.
Right calf has an increased circumference of 3.5 cm compared to the left, with visible erythema, local warmth, and marked tenderness along the deep posterior calf veins and on passive dorsiflexion.
Moderate unilateral pitting edema over the right lower leg and ankle; no pitting edema on the left lower extremity.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and symmetrical bilaterally.
No superficial skin abrasions, puncture wounds, insect bites, or spider angiomas on either lower extremity.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezing, crackles, or pleural friction rubs.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or third heart sound.
Normal jugular venous pressure without neck vein distention at 45 degrees.
Thyroid is normal in size, non-tender, and symmetrical without palpable nodules or bruits.
Abdomen is flat, soft, and non-tender without hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or shifting dullness.
